title: What must an offshore safety case say about workforce competence?
description: What the OPGGS (Safety) Regulations 2024 and NOPSEMA guidance require a safety case to show about workforce skills, training and competence offshore.
shortAnswer: Under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Safety) Regulations 2024, which commenced on June 12, 2025, the safety case for every offshore facility in Commonwealth waters must describe how the operator ensures each member of the workforce has the skills, training and ability for routine and non-routine tasks in normal, abnormal and emergency conditions and during changes. NOPSEMA assesses the safety case and expects contractors to be included and recognized units of competency to be considered.
keyTakeaways: Section 2.9 of the 2024 Regulations is the core competence provision: the safety case must describe how each member of the workforce gets the necessary skills, training and ability, including to respond during an emergency.

Section 2.8 adds that people in command of the facility and in charge of emergency procedures must have the necessary skills, training and ability, and section 2.10 requires workers to be competent in the permit to work system.
The 2024 Regulations were registered on December 6, 2024 and commenced on June 12, 2025, alongside amendments to the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006 passed in May 2024.
A safety case must be revised within 14 days before the end of each 5 year period after acceptance, and earlier on a change of circumstances or at NOPSEMA's request.

NOPSEMA's Safety Management System guidance note (November 25, 2025) says competencies should fit the scope and work environment, should include contractors, and should consider nationally and internationally recognized units of competency.
regulator: National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority (NOPSEMA)
appliesTo: Registered operators of offshore petroleum and greenhouse gas storage facilities in Commonwealth waters, including platforms, FPSOs, mobile drilling units and pipelines
Members of the workforce at a facility, including contractors
Offshore installation managers and persons in the emergency command structure
Diving contractors, diving supervisors and divers working on diving projects

sections.heading: Why does competence sit inside the offshore safety case?

blocks.text: Australia's offshore regime makes the operator describe, and NOPSEMA accept, how the facility will be run safely before work starts. NOPSEMA's [safety cases page](https://www.nopsema.gov.au/offshore-industry/safety/safety-cases-and-validation) states that a facility cannot be constructed, installed, operated, modified or decommissioned without a safety case in force for that stage, and that the [Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Safety) Regulations 2024](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2024L01588/asmade/text) set out what a safety case must contain.

Competence is therefore not a stand-alone training rule. It is a set of things the operator must describe in the safety case and then implement through its safety management system. Once accepted, the safety case becomes the standard against which NOPSEMA inspects. A training program that drifts from what the safety case describes is a compliance gap even if the training itself is sound.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Safety) Regulations 2024 as made and NOPSEMA guidance as at November 2026. NOPSEMA said it would revise its new guidance as required during the first 12 months after commencement. Check NOPSEMA's document hub for the current guidance note versions.

sections.heading: What does section 2.9 require about workforce competence?

blocks.text: Section 2.9, headed "Members of the workforce must be competent", requires the safety case to describe the means by which the operator will ensure that each member of the workforce has the necessary skills, training and ability for three things: to undertake routine and non-routine tasks reasonably given to them in normal operating conditions, in abnormal or emergency conditions, and during any changes to the facility; and to respond and react appropriately during an emergency at the level reasonably required of them.

The wording sets a scope that many onshore training programs do not reach. Competence must be defined for abnormal conditions and for changes to the facility, not only for steady state operations. A competence system that covers normal operating tasks and an annual emergency drill, but says nothing about plant modifications or degraded modes, is unlikely to satisfy NOPSEMA's assessors.

NOPSEMA's [Safety Management System guidance note](https://www.nopsema.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/N-04300-GN1052%20-%20Safety%20Management%20Systems%20%28A336401%29%20.pdf) adds that competency requirements must be established for each of those conditions, that competencies should be directly applicable to the scope, context and work environment of the personnel, and that this should include contractors. It says NOPSEMA expects operators to have given appropriate consideration to nationally and internationally recognized units of competency when developing their competency assurance processes.

sections.heading: What competence rules apply to command roles and permit to work?

blocks.text: Section 2.8 requires the safety case to specify the office in command of the facility and responsible for its safe operation, the office responsible for implementing and supervising emergency procedures, and the emergency command structure. Under section 2.8(2), the safety case must describe in detail how the operator ensures, as far as reasonably practicable, that those offices are continuously occupied while the facility operates and that each occupant "has the necessary skills, training and ability to perform the functions of the office or position".

NOPSEMA's guidance note identifies the person in command as typically the Offshore Installation Manager, or the Master where the facility is a vessel, and says the safety case should address leave and unplanned absences. That makes deputy and relief arrangements for the OIM a competence question, not only a rostering one.

Section 2.10 requires a documented permit to work system covering hot work, cold work and isolation, electrical work, confined space entry, work over water and diving. Under section 2.10(2), the system must identify the persons responsible for authorizing and supervising work and ensure that members of the workforce are competent in applying the permit to work system.

sections.heading: When must the safety case, and the competence arrangements in it, be revised?

blocks.text: Section 2.32 requires the operator to submit a revised safety case within 14 days before the end of the 5 year period beginning on the day NOPSEMA accepted it, and before the end of each later 5 year period, even if it has revised the safety case for other reasons in that period. Sections 2.30 and 2.31 add revision on a change of circumstances or operations and on NOPSEMA's request.

NOPSEMA's guidance note treats competence as part of the risk picture that management of change must track, alongside plant, procedures and barriers. It lists the human resources and competence levels required to maintain safe operations among the things a management of change process should follow. A significant change in crewing model, contractor or automation can therefore trigger both retraining and a safety case revision. The guide on [updating training when requirements change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) covers the training side.

sections.heading: What other workforce provisions arrived with the 2024 Regulations?

blocks.text: Section 2.15A requires the safety case to describe the measures in place to prevent sexual harassment, bullying and harassment at the facility, comply with relevant legislation, and report incidents to NOPSEMA. NOPSEMA's guidance says this applies to all safety cases from June 12, 2025, and suggests operators make administrative revisions to address it. Training on prevention and reporting is one way an operator can give effect to those measures, and the obligations connect to [psychosocial hazards training requirements](/regulations/psychosocial-hazards-training-requirements).

For diving projects, the Regulations rely on the Australian Diver Accreditation Scheme (ADAS). A diving contractor must not appoint a diving supervisor who is not qualified as a supervisor under ADAS and competent to supervise the operation, and must not allow a person to dive without a current ADAS qualification for the activities reasonably likely to be required. Both are strict liability offenses carrying 100 penalty units.

blocks.text: The table below is an original mapping of the competence related provisions of the 2024 Regulations to the role they cover, the review cycle, and the evidence a NOPSEMA inspector would expect to find in the safety management system. blocks.text: The difference between knowing a procedure and demonstrating it under emergency conditions is the subject of [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency). Records that link each competence claim to an assessment are also what the guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) recommends.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures a facility's roles, operating conditions and major accident event controls as a framework, then links each role to the knowledge and assessment points the safety case commits to. When a management of change alters a control or a crewing arrangement, the roles and competencies affected can be traced before the safety case is revised. See the context for [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Does NOPSEMA prescribe specific training courses for offshore workers?
faqs.a: The 2024 Regulations do not prescribe a general course list for facility workers. They require the safety case to describe how the operator ensures competence, and NOPSEMA's guidance says the regulations do not prescribe any particular standard or model for the safety management system. Diving is the main exception, where ADAS qualifications are mandatory.

faqs.q: Do contractors need to be covered in the safety case competence arrangements?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 2.9 applies to each member of the workforce at the facility, and NOPSEMA's Safety Management System guidance note says competencies should be directly applicable to the work environment and should include contractors. Procedures for personnel selection, training and competency management, including contractors, are listed among the controls a safety management system generally addresses.

faqs.q: Did the 2024 Regulations replace the earlier offshore safety regulations?
faqs.a: Yes. NOPSEMA announced that new work health and safety regulations would come into effect on June 12, 2025, following a Commonwealth review of the offshore safety regime and amendments to the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006 passed in May 2024. The commencement table in the 2024 Regulations confirms the whole instrument commenced on June 12, 2025.

faqs.q: Does the five yearly revision mean competence only needs review every five years?
faqs.a: No. Section 2.32 sets a backstop for revising the whole safety case. Competence must be maintained continuously through the safety management system, and changes to the facility, operations or workforce can require earlier revision under section 2.30. NOPSEMA's guidance lists the competence levels needed for safe operations among the things management of change should track.
